title: Vector helpers
text:
Vector helpers are evaluated once per group on whole columns. Use them as mutate(), filter(), and summarize() arguments. They follow R’s NA rules: a summary returns NA when its input has an NA unless naRm: true, ranks keep NA, and cumulative functions stay NA after the first NA.
The first argument is the input column. A string there is a column name. It can also be col('x'), another helper, or a row closure. Later arguments are values. ->map(fn ($value, $r) => ...) transforms a helper’s result row by row.

title: Vector helpers
text:
Summaries



Helper
Value




n()
Rows in the group


n_distinct('x', 'y')
Distinct values or combinations


sum, mean, median
As in R


sd, var_ (alias variance)
Sample statistics (n − 1)


quantile('x', 0.9), iqr('x')
Type 7 quantiles, R’s default


min, max
Smallest and largest values


first, last, nth('x', 2)
Values by position, with default:


any, all
Logical summaries with NA logic



With the phit extension loaded, mean, sd, var_, median, and quantile use it. Without it, they run in PHP. The test suite checks both against R.

title: Vector helpers
text:
Window functions







Helper
Value

row_number(), row_number('x')
Row numbers, or ranks with ties broken by position


min_rank, dense_rank
Ranks; wrap the column in desc() to reverse


percent_rank, cume_dist
Ranks scaled to [0, 1]


ntile('x', 4)
Buckets of near-equal size


cumsum, cumprod, cummin, cummax, cummean
Running values


cumall, cumany
Running logical values


consecutive_id('x')
A new id each time the value changes


order_by('t', cumsum('x'))
A window function evaluated in another order




PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv') |>
    filter(fn ($r) => $r->school === 'school-01') |>
    arrange('study_hours') |>
    mutate(
        prev: lag('score'),
        change: lag('score')->map(fn ($prev, $r) => $prev === null ? null : round($r->score - $prev, 2)),
        running_mean: cummean('score'),
        rank: min_rank(desc('score')),
        pct: percent_rank('score'),
        quartile: ntile('score', 4),
    ) |>
    select('study_hours', 'score', 'prev', 'change', 'running_mean', 'rank', 'pct', 'quartile') |>
    head(8);


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromCsv('schools.csv'))
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->school === 'school-01')
    ->arrange('study_hours')
    ->mutate(
        prev: lag('score'),
        change: lag('score')->map(fn ($prev, $r) => $prev === null ? null : round($r->score - $prev, 2)),
        running_mean: cummean('score'),
        rank: min_rank(desc('score')),
        pct: percent_rank('score'),
        quartile: ntile('score', 4),
    )
    ->select('study_hours', 'score', 'prev', 'change', 'running_mean', 'rank', 'pct', 'quartile')
    ->head(8);

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['state' => 'NC', 'visits' => 3],
    ['state' => 'NYC', 'visits' => null],
    ['state' => 'CA', 'visits' => 12],
    ['state' => null, 'visits' => 0],
]) |>
    mutate(
        name: recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'),
        visits: coalesce('visits', 0),
        busy: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visits > 5, 'yes', 'no'),
        capped: replace_when('visits', [fn ($r) => $r->visits > 10, 10]),
        any_flag: when_any(fn ($r) => $r->state === 'CA', fn ($r) => $r->visits === 0),
    );


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['state' => 'NC', 'visits' => 3],
    ['state' => 'NYC', 'visits' => null],
    ['state' => 'CA', 'visits' => 12],
    ['state' => null, 'visits' => 0],
]))
    ->mutate(
        name: recode_values('state', ['NC', 'North Carolina'], [['NY', 'NYC'], 'New York'], default: 'other'),
        visits: coalesce('visits', 0),
        busy: if_else(fn ($r) => $r->visits > 5, 'yes', 'no'),
        capped: replace_when('visits', [fn ($r) => $r->visits > 10, 10]),
        any_flag: when_any(fn ($r) => $r->state === 'CA', fn ($r) => $r->visits === 0),

title: tidyselect and across()
text:
Selectors pick columns by name, pattern, or type. They work in select(), relocate(), rename_with(), arrange(), distinct(), group_by(), count(), across(), pick(), and the tidyr functions.







Selector
Columns




'x', ['x', 'y']
By name

By name fragment; case-insensitive unless ignoreCase: false


matches('^x\\d+$')

num_range('x', 1, 3)
x1, x2, x3

All columns, the last column

Names from a list, strict or lenient


where('numeric'), where(fn ($values, $type, $name) => ...)
By type or predicate


group_cols()
The grouping columns


except(...)
Everything but these (dplyr’s -x)


any_selected(...), all_selected(...)

where() accepts 'numeric', 'integer', 'double', 'character', 'logical', 'factor', 'date', 'datetime', 'time', and 'list', or a Phibble\Type. 'numeric' selects integer and double columns. 'time' selects phibble’s time columns, R’s hms, and needs phibble 0.6 or later.

title: tidyselect and across()
Strings and dates
text: phplyr re-exports phibble’s stringr and lubridate functions. They build expressions, so they work in memory and, where a SQL translation exists, on database tables. Their results are checked against stringr 1.6.0 and lubridate 1.9.5.

title: Strings and dates
text:
Strings
As in stringr, a pattern is a regular expression. fixed('a.b') matches the text literally, and regex('ab', ignoreCase: true) sets options.







Function
Value




str_detect(x, p, negate:), str_starts, str_ends
Whether the pattern matches


str_count(x, p)
Number of matches


str_extract(x, p)
The first match, or NA


str_extract_all(x, p), str_split(x, p)
A list per row (a list-column)


str_split_i(x, p, i)
The i-th piece; negative counts from the end


str_replace(x, p, r), str_replace_all
Replace the first or every match; \1 refers to a group


str_pad(x, width, side:, pad:)
Pad to a width


str_trunc(x, width, side:, ellipsis:)
Truncate with an ellipsis


str_to_title, str_to_upper, str_to_lower
Change case


str_squish, str_trim(x, side)
Remove whitespace


str_length, str_sub(x, start, end)
Length and substrings



Strings are UTF-8. str_length(), str_sub(), str_pad(), and the other functions count UTF-8 characters, and the case functions change accented letters too.
str_replace, str_pad, and str_split have the names of PHP built-ins. In a file that imports them, write \str_replace() for the built-in.

title: Strings and dates
text:
Dates and times







Function
Value




ymd, dmy, mdy, ymd_hms, dmy_hms, mdy_hms (tz:)
Parse text; failures give NA


parse_date_time(x, ['Ymd HMS', 'dmY HMS'])
Parse with lubridate orders


year, month, day, yday, quarter, hour, minute, second
Parts


wday(x, weekStart:)
Day of the week; Sunday is 1 unless weekStart: 1


floor_date(x, unit), ceiling_date, round_date
Round to 'hour', '15 minutes', 'week', 'month', and so on


seconds(n) … years(n)
Periods: col('d')->add(months(1))


difftime(x, y, units:)
The difference as a number


with_tz(x, tz), force_tz(x, tz)
Change the displayed zone, or the zone itself


today(tz:), now(tz:)
The current date or time



The parsing functions return UTC date-times unless tz: names a zone, as in lubridate. PHP’s default time zone does not change the result. with_tz() keeps the instant and changes the zone it is shown in, and force_tz() keeps the clock time and changes the zone.
On a database table, a function without a SQL translation for that database loads the rows and runs in PHP, as Databases and expressions describes.
Month and year arithmetic that lands on a date that doesn’t exist, such as January 31 plus one month, gives NA, as in lubridate. Subtracting dates gives days, and subtracting datetimes gives seconds. Date columns stay dates through these functions.

title: Models
text:
lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer() fit models with phit. phit reads factor levels from the table, builds the model matrix from an R formula, and fits the model. phplyr adds no model code of its own.
The functions come from the phit extension or from phit-polyfill, its PHP port, and phplyr calls both the same way. phit’s Extension or polyfill page compares them. The extension is faster in phit-polyfill’s recorded benchmarks, which time phit’s matrix fitting functions:
Apple M5 Ultra, PHP 8.5.10 with OPcache on and the JIT off, both in one process. The polyfill’s linear mixed fits take time roughly proportional to the cube of the number of random coefficients.
CI runs phplyr’s tests with each implementation. Both runs compare lm() and glm() coefficients with R’s, and lmer() fixed effects with lme4’s.
Other named arguments go to phit’s function unchanged. phit’s documentation lists them and the formula syntax it accepts.

title: Models
text:
phit 0.3 and earlier
phit 0.3 and earlier name the functions fit_lm(), fit_glm(), fit_lmer(), and fit_glmer(). phplyr calls those names when the current ones are missing, so it works with phit 0.1 and later. phit 0.4 keeps the old names as deprecated aliases, which phplyr doesn’t call.

title: Models
Grouping
text:
group_by() sets the grouping columns. Selectors work, named arguments group by a computed column, and _add: true adds to the existing groups. _drop: false keeps groups for unused factor levels, so summarize() and count() return them with n() = 0, as dplyr does. ungroup() removes grouping, or only the named columns.
Groups are ordered like dplyr’s: sorted by key, factors by level order, and NA last. filter(), mutate(), summarize(), and the slice functions work within groups. _by: groups for a single call and returns an ungrouped table.

title: Grouping
Porting an R script
text:
A typical R analysis of the schools data, translated to PHP. It reads a CSV file, cleans and reshapes it, summarizes it, and fits a linear, a logistic, and a random-intercept model.
Data: schools.csv. The R script needs dplyr, tidyr, and lme4. The PHP script needs phplyr and, for the models, phit; see Models.

title: Porting an R script
text:
What changed in translation

Loading. read.csv() becomes DataFrame::fromCsv(), which infers column types like readr.
Pipes. On PHP 8.5, R’s |> stays |>. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, the pipeline becomes a method chain that starts with phplyr($t).
Column references. Bare names become strings, or col('x') inside expressions, so score - prior_score becomes col('score')->sub(col('prior_score')).
Conditions. case_when(x < 4 ~ "low", .default = "high") becomes case_when([col('x')->lt(4), 'low'], default: 'high').
Renaming in select. select(prior = prior_score) becomes select(['prior' => 'prior_score']).
Column sets. c(prior, final) becomes ['prior', 'final'].
Models. lm(), glm(), and lmer() take the same formulas. They return arrays, so coef() and fixef() become reads of coefficients.
Printing. DataFrames print in tibble’s format.

On a database table from Phibble\tbl(), the cleaning, counting, and grouped-summary steps run as SQL, because they use col() expressions and phplyr’s helpers. The reshaping step loads the rows into PHP. See Databases and expressions.

title: phplyr
text: Filter, transform, join, and reshape tables with dplyr- and tidyr-style functions. Use PHP 8.5 pipes, or method chains on PHP 8.3 and later.

title: phplyr
phplyr
text:
phplyr and phibble
The tables come from phibble, which Composer installs with phplyr. phplyr adds dplyr’s and tidyr’s functions on top of phibble’s table methods, so a pipeline runs on an in-memory DataFrame, on a database table as SQL, or on Polars.
phplyr has:

dplyr’s single-table and two-table functions, with grouped window functions, across(), column selectors, and join_by() conditions.
tidyr’s pivoting, completing, splitting, nesting, and list-column functions.
janitor’s clean_names(), remove_empty(), get_dupes(), and tabyl().
lm(), glm(), lmer(), and glmer(), which fit models with phit.

title: phplyr
text:
Install
composer require phpstats/phplyr
phplyr needs PHP 8.3 or later with the mbstring and PDO extensions. Installation lists the optional extensions, and Compatibility and limitations lists the dplyr features phplyr doesn’t have.

title: Gallery

Compatibility and limitations
text:
phplyr supports PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. The pipe operator |> is PHP 8.5 syntax. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, the same pipelines are method chains, or calls to pipe(). Installation lists the required and optional extensions.

Without phit or phit-polyfill, the model functions throw a RuntimeException that names the missing function. See Models.
Without intl, make_clean_names() transliterates with iconv, and some names can differ from janitor’s.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
phplyr supports PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. The pipe operator |> is PHP 8.5 syntax. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, the same pipelines are method chains, or calls to pipe(). Installation lists the required and optional extensions.

Without phit or phit-polyfill, the model functions throw a RuntimeException that names the missing function. See Models.
Without intl, make_clean_names() transliterates with iconv, and some names can differ from janitor’s.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Backends
A phplyr function calls the methods of phibble’s Table contract, so a pipeline runs on any table that implements it:

Phibble\DataFrame holds the data in PHP memory.
Phibble\tbl($pdo, 'table') builds SQL for SQLite, PostgreSQL, or MySQL. A function given a PHP closure, and an expression without a SQL translation, runs the query so far, loads the rows, and continues in memory. Databases and expressions lists those expressions.
Phibble\Polars\PolarsTable belongs to phibble and runs pipelines in Polars through the phpolars extension. A closure step converts the data to a DataFrame and back.

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Not supported

Bare column names and tidy evaluation. Columns are strings, and expressions are closures, helpers, or col() expressions.
mutate(_keep: 'used') and _keep: 'unused' with closures. These work with expression arguments such as col('x')->mul(2), whose columns phplyr can read. A PHP closure does not expose the columns it reads, so phplyr throws an InvalidArgumentException.
cur_data() and cur_data_all(), which dplyr has deprecated. Use pick().
Data frame columns and across(.unpack). pack() makes a column of named arrays.
The scoped _at, _if, and _all variants, such as mutate_at(). Use across().
janitor’s adorn_*() functions and three-way tabyl().

title: Compatibility and limitations
text:
Differences in behavior

_by sorts groups. dplyr keeps the order of first appearance for .by. phplyr sorts by key, as it does for group_by().
Strings are UTF-8. String functions count UTF-8 characters.
Date-times parse to UTC unless a function is given tz:, whatever PHP’s default time zone is, as in lubridate.
Models return arrays. lm() and the other model functions return phit’s result array, with R’s coefficient names in columns, in place of a model object.

title: Coming from dplyr
text: phplyr keeps dplyr’s and tidyr’s function names, argument names, and results. This page lists the differences that come from PHP syntax. Compatibility and limitations lists the dplyr features phplyr does not have.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
Syntax translation
In R, functions are chained with %>% or |>. In PHP 8.5, they are chained with |>. On PHP 8.3 and 8.4, they are methods of a chain: phplyr($t)->filter(...)->arrange(...). The table below shows single calls.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
Conventions

Positions are 1-based, as in R: pull(1) is the first column, pull(-1) the last, and slice(1, 3) the first and third rows of each group.
var() is var_(), because var is a reserved word in PHP. variance() is an alias.
summarise() and summarize() are the same function, as in dplyr.
count(), min(), max(), rename(), and other functions have the names of PHP built-ins. In a file that imports them, write \count() for the built-in. Imports lists them.
Group order follows dplyr: groups are sorted by key, factors by level order, and NA last. _by also sorts groups (dplyr keeps first-appearance order for .by).

An argument that dplyr or tidyr writes with a dot keeps it as a leading underscore, and a multi-word name is camelCase after it: .by is _by: and .keep_all is _keepAll:. There are sixteen options, and recode() also names its first parameter $_x, after dplyr’s .x:

Most of these verbs take the new columns as variadic named arguments, so the prefix keeps an option apart from a column of the same name, as the dot does in dplyr:

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$t |> mutate(m: mean('x'), _by: 'g');
$t |> mutate(by: 1);


phplyr($t)->mutate(m: mean('x'), _by: 'g');
phplyr($t)->mutate(by: 1);



The first call computes m within each group of g. The second makes a column called by.

An unprefixed named argument is always a column.
A prefixed name that isn’t an option for that verb is an error that names the options.
Every other argument is camelCase: naRm:, orderBy:, namesFrom:, and the rest.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
phplyr options and phibble methods
phplyr functions and phibble methods both take and return phibble tables, so a pipeline can use both. phibble’s methods have their own conventions:

A phibble method takes an array: $df->mutate(['z' => $expr]), $df->groupBy(['g']), $df->arrange([['x', 'desc']]). A phplyr function takes named arguments: mutate(z: ...), group_by('g'), arrange(desc('x')).
phibble methods have no underscored options. Grouping is a separate method call, and summarise(array $aggregates, ?string $groups) takes the .groups value as a second argument.
A phplyr helper such as mean('x') builds a phibble expression, which a database table can compile to SQL. See Databases and expressions.

title: Coming from dplyr
text:
across() functions
R passes a vector to every across() function. In phplyr, what a function receives depends on the function and the verb. See across().

title: Development
text:
The tests use Pest and run under PHP 8.3, 8.4, and 8.5. They call functions through pipe(), so they parse on every version. tests/Pipe/ holds the tests written with |>; bin/test leaves them out before PHP 8.5.
composer install
bin/test                 # loads .ext/libphit.dylib when present
NO_EXT=1 bin/test        # pure-PHP descriptive statistics
PHP=/path/to/php83 bin/test

title: Development
text:
Documentation
The site is a Quarto project in docs/. Code examples live in docs/examples/*.php. bin/docs-examples runs each one with docs/data as the working directory and writes docs/examples/_<name>.md with the code and its output, which the pages include. Rendering never executes PHP.
An example uses |>, and docs/examples/<name>.chain.php beside it is the same example as a method chain. bin/docs-examples runs both and fails if their output differs. The page shows the two in tabs labeled “PHP 8.5+” and “PHP 8.3–8.4”, with the output once. bin/docs-examples needs PHP 8.5, and it loads phit from .ext/libphit.dylib for the model examples.
Most examples leave out the require line and the imports, and bin/docs-examples adds them before it runs the code. An example that requires vendor/autoload.php itself is a complete script. It runs as written, so a missing import fails the run, and the page shows it without the opening tag and the require line. The first example, the porting script, and the pages in the Examples section (docs/examples/<slug>.qmd, with their code in docs/examples/pages/) are complete scripts. A subdirectory’s _prelude.php, such as the Gallery’s, replaces the generated prelude for its examples, and the page shows it once.
PHP=/path/to/php85 bin/docs-examples   # refresh example output
PHP=/path/to/php85 bin/render-docs     # examples, quarto render, publish to docs/
docs/_variables.yml names the latest release. The data URLs in the docs, the README, and site.json point at that tag, and a test fails until a new CHANGELOG release is matched there and in the README.
Commit the rendered HTML. phpstats.org imports it from the commit it pins and serves it at https://phplyr.phpstats.org/docs. GitHub Pages serves redirects to those pages, which .github/workflows/pages.yml builds with bin/pages-redirects.

title: Getting started
text:
A first script
A first pipeline on the overview page is a complete script, with the commands that install phplyr and download its data. The snippets on this page use its $schools table. The other examples’ CSV files are in docs/data.

title: Getting started
text:
Imports
phplyr’s functions are namespaced functions in Phplyr. Import the ones a file uses with use function. The snippets in the reference pages leave the imports out.
use Phibble\DataFrame;
use function Phplyr\{phplyr, filter, mutate, group_by};
use function Phplyr\{summarize, arrange, desc, n, mean};
A method chain needs phplyr() and the helpers it calls, such as n(), mean(), and desc(). The table functions are the chain’s methods, so they don’t need importing.
Some phplyr functions have the same names as PHP built-in functions. In a file that imports one of them, the bare name calls phplyr’s function. Write a leading backslash to call the built-in, as in \count($array).



phplyr functions
Where they are documented

Expressions

A file that doesn’t import these names is not affected.

title: Getting started
Getting started
text:
Pipelines
A table function such as filter(...) returns a closure that takes a table and returns a new one. A pipeline applies such closures in order.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


The pipe operator |> calls the closure on its right with the value on its left:
$out = $schools |>
    filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80) |>
    arrange(desc('score'));


phplyr($table) starts a method chain. Each method calls the phplyr function of the same name with the same arguments. A chained method is camelCase, so group_by() is ->groupBy() and n_groups() is ->nGroups(). get() returns the table:
$out = phplyr($schools)
    ->filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80)
    ->arrange(desc('score'))
    ->get();



The two forms give the same result, and the documentation shows both.
A method chain stays a chain while each method returns a table. These functions return something else, and the chain returns that value:







Functions
Return




pull(), group_vars(), group_size(), group_indices(), group_rows(), group_split(), group_map()
An array


n_groups()
An integer


setequal()
A boolean


show_query()
The SQL string


lm(), glm(), lmer(), glmer()
phit’s result array



echo prints a chain’s table without get(). ->pipe($closure) applies a closure of your own and continues the chain with its result.
pipe() applies closures in order on every PHP version:
$out = pipe($schools, filter(fn ($r) => $r->score > 80), arrange(desc('score')));

title: Getting started
text:
Named arguments and options
Functions that create columns name them with PHP named arguments: mutate(total: ...), summarize(n: n()). An option that dplyr writes with a leading dot, such as .by, is written with a leading underscore, such as _by:. Any other named argument is a column, so mutate(_before: 'id') places the new columns and mutate(before: 1) makes a column called before. Underscored arguments lists them.
PHP does not allow positional arguments after named ones. Put across() and other positional arguments first: summarize(across(...), n: n()).

title: Getting started
text:
Printing and inspecting
echo prints a table. glimpse() prints one line per column and returns the table unchanged, so it can sit inside a pipeline. pull('x') returns a column as a PHP array, and $table->toRows() returns every row as an array.

title: Performance
text:
Choosing a backend

In-memory DataFrame suits data that fits in memory. In the grouped summary above, expression arguments took 0.17 s and closures 0.40 s, because phibble computes expressions in one pass without building a table per group.
A database table (Phibble\tbl()) avoids loading the data into PHP. With expressions, filter() and summarise() run in the database, and only the result reaches PHP. These timings exclude loading the data.
Pipelines that return every row (mutate(), arrange(), unfiltered joins) spend most of their database time transferring rows to PHP.
Closures on a database table load all rows first and then run in memory. Use col() expressions and phplyr’s helpers to keep the work in SQL.
SQLite columns need declared types. PDO binds values as strings. In an untyped column, SQLite stores them as text and compares numbers as text.
PolarsTable (phibble’s Polars backend, on the phpolars extension) runs expressions in Polars. A closure step converts the data to a DataFrame and back, so the closure workloads above were slower on PolarsTable than on DataFrame.

A: filter, join a store lookup, two-key summarise, then a ranking window.
B: grouped lag(orderBy:), cumsum(), and a share of the group total over all rows.
C: pipeline A with a closure in filter(). It has no dplyr version, because its closure is PHP code.

phplyr’s helpers build inspectable expressions whenever their arguments are column names, literals, or other helpers. col('x') refers to a column, and methods combine expressions with operators:
filter(col('price')->mul(1.1)->gt(100), col('brand')->isIn(['a', 'b']))
mutate(margin: col('price')->sub(col('cost'))->div(col('price')))
mutate(dev: col('score')->sub(mean('score')))      // mean() recycles per group

title: Databases and expressions
janitor
text: phplyr has the single-table functions from R’s janitor package, with janitor 2.2’s rules.

title: janitor
text:
Clean names
clean_names() renames every column of a table, and make_clean_names() applies the same rules to a list of strings. The rules follow janitor’s defaults:

% becomes percent, # becomes number, and quotes are dropped.
Accented and non-Latin characters are transliterated to ASCII: Café becomes cafe, straße becomes strasse, and αβγ becomes abg.
Spaces and punctuation become single underscores, and leading and trailing ones are dropped.
Case changes split words: camelCaseVar becomes camel_case_var, and HTMLParser becomes html_parser. Digits stay attached to their word.
A name that would start with a digit gets an x prefix, and an empty name becomes x.
A repeated name gets _2, _3, and so on, in order of appearance.

Transliteration uses ext-intl, which gives the same results as janitor’s stringi. Without ext-intl, phplyr falls back to iconv, and some names can differ from janitor’s.
make_clean_names(['First Name', 'first_name', '% Done', '1st Place']);
// ['first_name', 'first_name_2', 'percent_done', 'x1st_place']

pipe($survey, clean_names());

title: janitor
text:
Remove empty rows and columns
remove_empty() drops rows and columns that are entirely NA. Pass 'rows' or 'cols' to drop only one kind. With cutoff below 1, a row or column is kept when its share of non-NA values is above the cutoff. A cutoff works with only one of 'rows' and 'cols'. An empty string is a value, as in R.

title: janitor
text:
Duplicates
get_dupes('email') returns the rows whose values in the given columns appear more than once. The result has the given columns first, then dupe_count, then the other columns. Rows are sorted by dupe_count (descending) and then by the given columns. With no columns, every column is used. A grouped table keeps its groups, but duplicates are found across the whole table.

title: janitor
text:
Frequency tables
tabyl('g') counts the values of one column. The result has the values, n, and percent. When the column has NAs, valid_percent gives each share with NA left out. showNa: false drops the NA row instead.
tabyl('g', 'h') counts pairs of values. It has one row per value of g and one column of counts per value of h. An NA in h is counted in the NA_ column, and an empty string in the emptystring_ column.
Values are sorted as in dplyr’s count(), with NA last. Factors keep their level order, and showMissingLevels: false leaves out unused levels.
pipe($people, tabyl('region'));
pipe($people, tabyl('region', 'smoker', showNa: false));
janitor’s adorn_*() functions and three-way tables are not included.

Single-table functions

title: tidyr
text:
Pivoting
pivot_longer(cols) turns the selected columns into rows of names and values.








Option
Default
Effect

'name'

'value'

Drop rows whose values are all NA

pivot_wider() spreads names and values into columns.








Option

Effect

'name', 'value'
Columns that supply the new names and their values


idCols

Columns that identify the output rows

Without valuesFn, duplicate cells turn the value columns into list-columns and trigger a PHP warning with tidyr’s message.
build_longer_spec() and build_wider_spec() return tidyr’s pivot spec as a table, and pivot_longer_spec() and pivot_wider_spec() run an edited one. The superseded gather() and spread() are also available.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


$scores = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['student' => 'ann', 'wk1' => 10, 'wk2' => null, 'wk3' => 30],
    ['student' => 'bob', 'wk1' => 7, 'wk2' => 8, 'wk3' => 9],
]);

$long = $scores |> pivot_longer(starts_with('wk'), namesTo: 'week', namesPrefix: 'wk', valuesTo: 'points', valuesDropNa: true);
echo $long;

echo "\n", $long |> pivot_wider(namesFrom: 'week', valuesFrom: 'points', namesPrefix: 'week_', valuesFill: 0, namesSort: true);


$scores = DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['student' => 'ann', 'wk1' => 10, 'wk2' => null, 'wk3' => 30],
    ['student' => 'bob', 'wk1' => 7, 'wk2' => 8, 'wk3' => 9],
]);

$long = phplyr($scores)->pivotLonger(starts_with('wk'), namesTo: 'week', namesPrefix: 'wk', valuesTo: 'points', valuesDropNa: true)->get();
echo $long;

echo "\n", phplyr($long)->pivotWider(namesFrom: 'week', valuesFrom: 'points', namesPrefix: 'week_', valuesFill: 0, namesSort: true);

title: tidyr
text:
Missing combinations and values
complete() adds missing combinations of the given columns and fills other columns with NA, or with values from fill:. A column name expands to its unique values (a factor to its levels), nesting() keeps only combinations that occur, and a named list supplies the values. It works within groups. expand() returns only the combinations, and crossing() and expand_grid() build a new table from lists.

PHP 8.5+PHP 8.3–8.4


echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 1, 'sales' => 10],
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 3, 'sales' => 12],
    ['shop' => 'south', 'month' => 2, 'sales' => 7],
]) |>
    complete('shop', month: [1, 2, 3], fill: ['sales' => 0]);


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 1, 'sales' => 10],
    ['shop' => 'north', 'month' => 3, 'sales' => 12],
    ['shop' => 'south', 'month' => 2, 'sales' => 7],
]))
    ->complete('shop', month: [1, 2, 3], fill: ['sales' => 0]);

  shop  month sales
  <chr> <int> <int>
1 north     1    10
2 north     2     0
3 north     3    12
4 south     1     0
5 south     2     7
6 south     3     0
fill() carries values down or up over NA within groups (_direction: 'down' | 'up' | 'downup' | 'updown'). drop_na() drops rows with NA in the given columns, and replace_na() replaces NA per column.

echo DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['quarter' => 'Q1', 'year' => 2024, 'sales' => 10],
    ['quarter' => 'Q2', 'year' => null, 'sales' => null],
    ['quarter' => 'Q3', 'year' => null, 'sales' => 14],
]) |>
    fill('year') |>
    replace_na(['sales' => 0]);


echo phplyr(DataFrame::fromRows([
    ['quarter' => 'Q1', 'year' => 2024, 'sales' => 10],
    ['quarter' => 'Q2', 'year' => null, 'sales' => null],
    ['quarter' => 'Q3', 'year' => null, 'sales' => 14],
]))
    ->fill('year')
    ->replaceNa(['sales' => 0]);

text:
join_by()
join_by() builds dplyr’s join specifications. A string is an equality on the same column name, ['a' => 'b'] maps names, and a comparison of two col() expressions compares x’s column (left) with y’s (right). Every condition must hold.
join_by('id', col('t')->ge(col('start')), col('t')->lt(col('end')))
join_by('id', between('t', 'start', 'end'))        // start and end are y's columns
join_by('id', closest(col('t')->ge(col('start'))))  // the latest start at or before t
join_by(within('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))         // x's interval inside y's
join_by(overlaps('lo', 'hi', 'start', 'end'))
For inequality, rolling, and overlap joins, keep defaults to dplyr’s behavior: equality keys are merged and the columns in other conditions are kept from both tables. keep: false is an error for these joins. Database tables run them in SQL, except right and full rolling joins, which load the rows.
nest_join() keeps every row of x and adds a list-column (name:, default 'data') holding each row’s matching rows of y as a table.
